conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: The claim is false/unsupported.** Soursop (graviola/Annona muricata) does not "cure" cancer in humans. While laboratory (in vitro/animal) studies show that compounds in soursop, particularly acetogenins like annonacin, have cytotoxic effects on cancer cells, there are no completed, reliable human clinical trials demonstrating that soursop treats or cures cancer in people. Major medical fact-checkers and cancer authorities uniformly reject the cure claim: PolitiFact concludes "there haven't been human studies," and Wikipedia states plainly there is "not enough reliable medical evidence that it is effective for treating cancer or any disease," citing Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center and Cancer Research UK (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop). Snopes similarly rates the "10,000 times more effective than chemo" claim false, noting that lab-based anticancer activity does not translate to a proven human cure (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/). PolitiFact's fact-check reached the same conclusion after consulting oncologists (https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/).

Additionally, safety concerns exist: soursop's active compound annonacin is neurotoxic and has been linked to an atypical form of Parkinson's disease in populations with high consumption, particularly in the French West Indies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annonacin). This raises concern about promoting soursop as an unsupervised "cure," since it could pose neurological risks without proven anticancer benefit in humans.

**Bottom line:** Soursop shows promising anticancer activity in preclinical (lab/animal) research, but no rigorous human trials confirm it cures or effectively treats cancer, and consuming it carries potential neurotoxic risks. Cancer patients should not substitute soursop for evidence-based medical treatment and should consult oncologists before using it as a supplement.
